---
title: "1. What Google Cloud Is"
description: "Organizations, folders, projects, billing accounts, regions and zones: where your things live in Google Cloud and who pays for them."
---

Before the Lemonade Stand can rent a single computer from Google, you need three answers. **Where** will its things live? **Who** pays for them? **Which city** are they in? This lesson answers all three.

## The problem

The Lemonade Stand runs on two laptops in the back room. When one laptop overheats on a hot day, the menu page disappears and customers walk away. The owner wants to rent Google's computers instead.

The first time they open the Google Cloud console, they meet unfamiliar words: *organization*, *project ID*, *billing account*, *region*, *zone*. Every later lesson creates things inside these containers, so we learn them first.

## Explain it like I'm ten

::: {.callout-tip}
Think of Google Cloud as a **huge school**.

- The **organization** is the whole school.
- **Folders** are the wings of the school, such as "Year 5" or "Science wing".
- A **project** is one **classroom**. Each classroom has its own door key, its own supply cupboard and its own bill for pencils. Whatever you build for the Lemonade Stand goes into the classroom called `lemonade-stand-dev`.
- **Resources** are the desks, books and computers inside the classroom.
- The **billing account** is the parent who pays for the pencils. One parent can pay for several classrooms.

The school has buildings in many cities. A **region** is a city, such as London. A **zone** is one separate building in that city, with its own power and cooling. If one building has a power cut, the other buildings in the same city keep working.

Luiz André Barroso and Urs Hölzle, two of the engineers who designed Google's datacenters, wrote a famous book called [*The Datacenter as a Computer*](https://research.google/pubs/the-datacenter-as-a-computer-designing-warehouse-scale-machines/) (first edition 2009). Their big idea: a whole warehouse full of machines behaves like **one giant computer**. When you use Google Cloud, you rent a tiny slice of that giant computer.
:::

## The idea, precisely

### The resource hierarchy

Everything in Google Cloud sits in a tree:

```text
Organization  example.com                      (optional: needs Google Workspace or Cloud Identity)
└── Folder    shop                             (optional: folders can nest up to 10 levels)
    └── Project  lemonade-stand-dev            (required: every resource belongs to exactly one project)
        ├── Cloud Run service   lemonade-web
        ├── Storage bucket      lemonade-stand-dev-menu
        └── VM                  web1
```

- An **organization** is the root. It exists only if you have a company domain managed by Google Workspace or Cloud Identity. A personal Gmail account has no organization, so its projects have no parent, and that is fine for learning.
- A **folder** groups projects, for example by team or by environment (`dev`, `prod`).
- A **project** is the basic container. APIs, billing, permissions and quotas are all switched on per project.
- A **resource** is a real thing you create: a VM, a bucket, a database.

Permissions set high in the tree flow **down** to everything below. Lesson 3 uses this.

### A project has three names

| Field | Example | Who chooses it | Unique? | Can change? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Project name | `Lemonade Stand Dev` | you | no | yes |
| Project ID | `lemonade-stand-dev` | you, at creation | yes, across **all** of Google Cloud | **never** |
| Project number | `123456789012` | Google | yes | never |

Project ID rules: 6 to 30 characters, made of lowercase letters, digits and hyphens. It must start with a letter and must not end with a hyphen. Once a project is deleted, its ID can never be used again. Commands almost always want the **project ID**.

### Billing accounts

A **billing account** holds a payment method. You **link** a project to it. A project with no billing account can only use free things. A project can link to at most one billing account, but one billing account can pay for many projects.

### Regions and zones

| Term | Example | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Region | `europe-west2` | a geographic place (London) with several zones |
| Zone | `europe-west2-a` | one isolated deployment area inside a region: its own power, cooling and network |

Naming convention: a region is `<area>-<direction><number>`, and a zone is the region plus `-` and a letter. `europe-west2` has the zones `europe-west2-a`, `europe-west2-b` and `europe-west2-c`.

### Global, regional and zonal resources

Every resource has a **scope**. The scope tells you which outage can take it down.

| Scope | Lives in | Lemonade examples |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zonal | one zone | a VM (`web1`), a zonal persistent disk |
| Regional | all zones of one region | a subnet, a Cloud Run service, a high-availability Cloud SQL instance |
| Global | everywhere | a VPC network, firewall rules, VM images |

The rule "a zonal resource dies with its zone" can be written in one line.

$$
\operatorname{up}(x, z) \iff Z(x) \setminus \lbrace z \rbrace \neq \emptyset
$$

where:

- $x$ is one resource, such as the VM `web1`;
- $z$ is the zone that has an outage;
- $Z(x)$ is the set of zones the resource runs in;
- $\setminus$ means "remove", so $Z(x) \setminus \lbrace z \rbrace$ is the set of zones still working for $x$;
- $\emptyset$ is the empty set, so "$\neq \emptyset$" means "at least one zone is left";
- $\iff$ means "exactly when";
- $\operatorname{up}(x, z)$ is true when $x$ keeps working during the outage of $z$.

Example: the zone `europe-west2-a` goes down.

- `web1` is zonal: $Z(\texttt{web1}) = \lbrace a \rbrace$. Then $\lbrace a \rbrace \setminus \lbrace a \rbrace = \emptyset$, so $\operatorname{up}$ is false. The menu VM is down.
- The Cloud Run service is regional: $Z(\texttt{lemonade-web}) = \lbrace a, b, c \rbrace$. Then $\lbrace a, b, c \rbrace \setminus \lbrace a \rbrace = \lbrace b, c \rbrace \neq \emptyset$, so $\operatorname{up}$ is true. Customers still see the menu.

The model assumes that a regional service moves its work to the healthy zones by itself. Google-managed regional services such as Cloud Run do this. For your own VMs, you must place copies in two zones yourself.

### APIs must be switched on

Each Google Cloud product is an API with a service name, such as `run.googleapis.com`. A new project has most APIs **off**. If you call an API that is off, you get an error that names the service and says it "has not been used in project … or it is disabled". Enable it once per project.

## Command reference

| Command or flag | What it does | Rule / convention | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `gcloud projects create` | creates a project | the ID is permanent; choose it carefully | `gcloud projects create lemonade-stand-dev --name="Lemonade Stand Dev"` |
| `--folder`, `--organization` | puts the new project under a parent | needs an organization | `--folder=345678901234` |
| `gcloud projects list` | lists projects you can see | add `--format` for scripts | `gcloud projects list --format="value(projectId)"` |
| `gcloud projects describe` | shows ID, name, number, state | the number is a string | `gcloud projects describe lemonade-stand-dev` |
| `gcloud projects delete` | shuts a project down | it is fully deleted after 30 days | `gcloud projects delete lemonade-stand-dev` |
| `gcloud projects undelete` | brings back a shut-down project | only within those 30 days | `gcloud projects undelete lemonade-stand-dev` |
| `gcloud billing accounts list` | shows billing accounts you can use | IDs look like `XXXXXX-XXXXXX-XXXXXX` | `gcloud billing accounts list` |
| `gcloud billing projects link` | links a project to a billing account | needed before paid APIs work | `gcloud billing projects link lemonade-stand-dev --billing-account=01A2B3-C4D5E6-F7A8B9` |
| `gcloud services enable` | turns an API on for the project | enable only what you use | `gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com` |
| `gcloud services list --enabled` | shows the APIs that are on | `--available` shows all | `gcloud services list --enabled` |
| `gcloud compute regions list` | lists regions | needs the Compute API enabled | `gcloud compute regions list` |
| `gcloud compute zones list` | lists zones | filter by region | `gcloud compute zones list --filter="region:europe-west2"` |
| `gcloud resource-manager folders create` | creates a folder | needs an organization | `gcloud resource-manager folders create --display-name=shop --organization=987654321098` |

## Worked example: a home for the Lemonade Stand

```bash
gcloud projects create lemonade-stand-dev --name="Lemonade Stand Dev"
gcloud billing projects link lemonade-stand-dev --billing-account=01A2B3-C4D5E6-F7A8B9
gcloud services enable compute.googleapis.com --project=lemonade-stand-dev
gcloud compute zones list --filter="region:europe-west2" --project=lemonade-stand-dev
```

Illustrative output of the last two commands (no account was used to write this book, but the format matches the real CLI):

```text
$ gcloud projects describe lemonade-stand-dev
createTime: '2026-11-25T09:00:00.000Z'
lifecycleState: ACTIVE
name: Lemonade Stand Dev
projectId: lemonade-stand-dev
projectNumber: '123456789012'

$ gcloud compute zones list --filter="region:europe-west2"
NAME            REGION        STATUS  NEXT_MAINTENANCE  TURNDOWN_DATE
europe-west2-c  europe-west2  UP
europe-west2-b  europe-west2  UP
europe-west2-a  europe-west2  UP
```

Read it like this: one project, one ID you chose, one number Google chose, and three London buildings to put things in.

When you are done experimenting, one command removes **everything** in the project:

```bash
gcloud projects delete lemonade-stand-dev
```

## Rules and conventions

- One project per environment: `lemonade-stand-dev`, `lemonade-stand-prod`. Deleting a project is the cleanest way to clean up.
- Put the environment at the end of the project ID, because the ID is permanent and globally unique.
- Pick one region near your customers and keep it everywhere. This book uses `europe-west2` (London).
- Treat zones as failure domains. Anything that must survive a zone outage needs two zones or a regional service.
- Enable only the APIs you use. Each enabled API is something else that can be called in the project.
- Link a billing account and create a **budget alert** (lesson 9) before creating paid resources.

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Using the project **name** where an ID is expected | `The project property is set to the empty string` or `project not found` | use `projectId`, e.g. `lemonade-stand-dev` |
| Choosing an ID that is already taken | `The project ID you specified is already in use by another project` | add a suffix: `lemonade-stand-dev-7f3` |
| Forgetting to link billing | `Billing account for project … is not found` when enabling paid APIs | `gcloud billing projects link …` |
| Calling an API that is off | `… has not been used in project 123456789012 before or it is disabled` | `gcloud services enable <service>` |
| One VM in one zone for something important | the menu disappears during a zone outage | use a regional service (Cloud Run) or VMs in two zones |
| Mixing up region and zone flags | `Invalid value for [--zone]: europe-west2` | zones end with a letter: `europe-west2-a` |

## Mathematical Abstraction

The hierarchy is a **tree**, so every resource has exactly one parent, and the chain of parents ends at the top. That chain is the resource's path.

$$
\operatorname{path}(r) = \big( r,\ \operatorname{parent}(r),\ \operatorname{parent}(\operatorname{parent}(r)),\ \dots \big)
$$

where:

- $r$ is any resource, folder or project;
- $\operatorname{parent}(r)$ is the container directly above $r$ (a project's parent is a folder or the organization; a project with no organization has no parent);
- the list stops when it reaches a node with no parent;
- $\operatorname{path}(r)$ is the whole chain from $r$ up to the top.

Example: $\operatorname{path}(\texttt{lemonade-web}) = (\texttt{lemonade-web},\ \texttt{lemonade-stand-dev},\ \texttt{shop},\ \texttt{example.com})$. That is 4 nodes: the service, its project, its folder and the organization. Lesson 3 shows that permissions on any of these 4 nodes apply to the service.

Billing is a **function** from projects to billing accounts:

$$
\beta : P \to B \cup \lbrace \bot \rbrace, \qquad \operatorname{canPay}(p) \iff \beta(p) \neq \bot
$$

where:

- $P$ is the set of your projects and $B$ is the set of billing accounts;
- $\beta(p)$ is the billing account linked to project $p$;
- $\bot$ ("bottom") stands for "no billing account linked";
- "$\to$" says that each project maps to exactly **one** value, so a project never has two billing accounts;
- $\operatorname{canPay}(p)$ is true when the project can use paid services.

Example: $\beta(\texttt{lemonade-stand-dev}) = \texttt{01A2B3-C4D5E6-F7A8B9}$, which is not $\bot$, so paid services work. A brand-new project `lemonade-stand-test` that nobody linked has $\beta = \bot$, so `gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com` fails there. Two projects can map to the same account: $\beta(\texttt{lemonade-stand-dev}) = \beta(\texttt{lemonade-stand-prod})$ is allowed.

The zone rule from earlier completes the picture: the tree decides **who** controls a resource, $\beta$ decides **who pays**, and $Z(x)$ decides **which outages** it survives.
